newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle crew prepares for robot arm test.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle crew prepares for robot arm test.

text.p: The crew of the space shuttle Discovery prepared on Friday to try out a prototype robot arm for the proposed international space station after releasing a satellite to gauge ozone depletion.

Astronaut Jan Davis was to perform the first test of a 5-foot-long (150 cm) dextrous robot arm, which is designed to tend experiments mounted to the outside of a Japanese laboratory module at the planned space station.
The space station, which will be built in orbit, has been beset with delays. It was supposed to be assembled in space later this year but has been postponed until 1998.

Eight hours after blasting off from Florida on Thursday, the shuttle crew achieved their primary objective, the release of a German-built satellite that will gauge ozone depletion in the Earth's upper atmosphere.
Early on Friday, the astronauts could see the 7,000-pound (3,200-kg) spacecraft, known as CRISTA-SPAS, trailing Discovery by about 40 miles (65 km).
"CRISTA is awfully beautiful in the sunrise," one of the astronauts told mission control. The spacecraft will be retrieved by the shuttle on Aug. 16.
Other tasks planned during the 11-day mission included observations of Comet Hale-Bopp, monitoring of vegetation on Earth, and the growth of colon cancer cells for medical research.
Discovery is due to return to Earth at the Florida spaceport on Aug. 18.
